utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody is here. The interpreters, can you hear me? I hear you. I should like to say good morning to the counsel for the Prosecution, and counsel for Defence, and the witness, and the accused, and without further adieu, I should like Witness N to stand up. Can you hear me? Witness, can you hear me? It is the President who is addressing you in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, first you have to see whether that is your name. This is the piece of paper, so will you please indicate whether this is your name. But do not pronounce it aloud, because there are people in the public gallery, listening to you. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, will you stay on your feet and take the solemn declaration. You will read it in your mother tongue. We are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may now be seated. We shall be calling you Witness N, because we have taken protective measures at your request. You were called by the Prosecution, which is to your right, to testify in a case against the accused, Goran Jelisic, and he is to your left. After the Prosecution has examined you and asked you all the questions they want to, you'll also be asked some questions by the Defence. You are now before the Judges. You have nothing to fear. You can speak very freely, and we hope that will make you feel good. Mr. Nice, the floor is yours. No, it is Mr. Tochilovsky. It is Mr. Tochilovsky who will be asking you some questions. Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Could you put the summary of the witness statement in front of him? Thank you. Examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness N, this is the summary you had an opportunity to read and recognise as a correct summary of your statement given to the OTP; is it right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness N, did you live in Brcko before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, on May the 1st, 1992, that a well-armed group of men came to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I do, yes. I remember it from stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any changes in the local radio broadcast after May the 1st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Serb Radio Brcko. It was a regular radio station before the war, and then they renamed it the Serb Radio Brcko, and then it began to broadcast some programmes and things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were houses looted at that time after May the 1st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Right away, as from the beginning, that is, as of the 1st of May when war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as soon as the war broke out, the systematic looting of houses started. First they looted houses of people who were employed abroad, and they presumably had very reliable information as to which houses were empty, which owners were away. And those first ones who came, they took things which were more valuable or, rather, those which were lighter but more valuable and could sell easier and better, and we had an opportunity to see that. In the beginning, they did it only at night-time, but then it went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who looted the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, it was armed soldiers or some special forces who came from Serbia or from somewhere, I don't know where, and they looted. They stole the most valuable things. But then the local people -- I mean what was left by these, the locals took away the rest of the things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On May 5th, 1992, did the radio broadcast that all Muslims and Croats should gather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't really say if it was broadcast by radio, but local Serbs, those who were there and those who were involved with those troops, they told us that they had to evacuate us from there because it was a war operations area, and we sort of accepted that. But then it turned out not to be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and other people go to the Laser Company, Laser Bus Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, that area where I used to live, we were taken to that bus company called Laser, and then I don't know whether they were elsewhere too, but I know that they took them to the barracks and here and there. But I cannot confirm that. From the Laser, they only transferred elderly people, that is, over 60, and women and children. They transferred them to the territory over near Celic and places like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While at Laser Company, were you allowed to leave the area of the company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: We were guarded. The first day, I remember, when I arrived there, we were guarded by local Serbs wearing olive-Gary SMB uniforms. We were not allowed to leave the compound of the company, but they did allow us to use a part of that compound around the canteen where we were kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any food available to those who were detained at Laser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, some acquaintances, some Serbs whom I knew from before who worked with me, they brought and gave me, and a fellow worker gave me some bread, I believe half a kilogram of bread. I don't really remember if they gave us any food, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you kept at Laser Company without any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, two or three days. That is how long I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened on the second night at Laser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: The second night in Laser. Well, it was when I suffered a shock. That is, I saw certain things which I had never experienced in my life before, because all of us who were there simply did not think that it would be just as bad as it could get. That night, Mr. Goran Jelisic, with two of his chums, turned up. I believe that they still had masks over their faces, that is, masks where there were only slits for the eyes. In a rather harsh voice, he said, "Muslims, in case you didn't know, my name is Goran Jelisic, nicknamed Adolf. I've killed 80 Muslims so far, and I'll finish all of you too." Then they started calling out some surnames. If I remember properly, Causevic, I remember that particular surname because they were kind of organisers in the SDA party and things like that. And then they began to beat people. They were asking for documents, for money from us, and there were screams and blows. Then after awhile they left and I can't tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On May 8th, were you and some other people taken to the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Jelisic, who called himself "Adolf"? Did you see him at the camp upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court the circumstances in which you saw him again upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, we were transferred from Laser to Luka. It was four or five bus loads, if I can remember properly. It was there that I saw Mr. Goran Jelisic for a second time. As soon as we got off the buses, our identity documents or, rather, any documents, any personal papers we had were taken away from us, or whatever personal luggage we had with us, a bag or something like that. Then -- I don't know how to put it, really -- that massive killing of people began. Then calling people out, provoking beatings, blows, and killings which were carried out by Jelisic. That was my second encounter with him, the second chance I had seeing him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to two brothers from Zvornik at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, yes. That has stuck in my memory somehow, because those guys were really young and they looked well. They stuck in my mind. I believe it was right away, as soon as we arrived. Jelisic called them out and began cursing and saying, "You've come from Zvornik to provoke war here." We heard -- when he took him out from the hangar, as you call it, where we were put up, and we heard people being beaten, who were crying with pain, moaning. I don't know how to put it. After that we heard shots. So I inferred that they had been killed. They were the first ones who were killed after my arrival in Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those two brothers interrogated, went through an interrogation before they were taken out and killed, or were they just called out and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, will you please remember what Mr. Greaves said yesterday? Will you please try to focus your questions on what you're seeking to prove, that is, the elements of genocide. May I remind you that this murder was confessed to, that the accused confessed to this murder and it was Count 17. Now you can move on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were those people interrogated before they were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move the bodies of those killed, while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies did you yourself move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I cannot really be 100 per cent sure, whether it was 12 or 15 bodies which I had to carry, but that was about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other detainees move the bodies as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of wounds those bodies had when you moved the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: The bodies that I carried, and we usually took them away in foursomes, that is, four people to carry the dead, they more often than not had injuries from blows. They were killed, as I tend to put it, in the same way; that is, with a shot at the back of their heads, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those prisoners who were taken out and never returned killed? Were those prisoners selected from others, if they were selected, and on which principle and how were they selected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, in my judgement -- I don't know how to put it -- they singled out first men with a particular surname or perhaps people who had nothing to do with it, that is, they were people of the same surname and who were not related or anything, but more or less, people who were prominent in the SDA leadership in Brcko at the time, such as, for instance, the surname such as Causevic and other surnames. In the beginning, they mostly took those people out. There were also instances when they took out people -- I don't really know. I mean, you know, they just took out people because they liked their looks or because they liked something or because they simply -- that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from seeing people taken out, killed, apart from seeing the bodies you moved, did you see any killings yourself, killings by Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was like this: On the second day at Luka, I began to carry the bodies of the killed. On my way back -- and I believe I've indicated on the sketch -- we took those people to a particular place where we would leave the bodies of the killed there and come back to that hangar. As we came near the hangar, near the entrance into the hangar, Jelisic took out a young man whom I knew by sight. I did not live in Brcko for quite some time. I had arrived there only of late. I remember the face of that young man sticks in my memory to this day. He was very thin, he was shorter than I, and he didn't have much hair. I could see by his looks that he had been beaten before, because he had bruises and he seemed very depressed and silent. Jelisic was taking him out of the hangar and took him to the grate -- I also indicated that place -- and he fired. This lad, he never put up any resistance as he was taken out. He was quite quiet, quite subdued. I don't know whether it was fear or depression, but did he not resist. He did not, whether he accepted his fate or something. At that moment he fired at his head or, rather, he made him lean over that grate -- I don't know how to put it -- and fired at his head, and told us, "Don't go in. There's no need for you to go in. You can carry this one too straightaway." Naturally, we did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he told you to take the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another killing you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. I saw yet another murder committed by Mr. Jelisic. That was a few days later. A group of us was taken to the police station, it was called MUP, Ministry of the Interior, to clear the broken glass, the splinters following the detonation on the bridge over the Sava. As they were coming out of the hangar, somebody comes, a policemen or some escorts come to take us there. Then we were coming out, but Jelisic had brought, I believe from the police station, an elderly man. At that time, I believe, he used a car, Zastava 101. If I remember properly, it was a police vehicle. It belonged to MUP. He dragged, brutally, the man from that car, accompanied by his usual -- by his routine vituperations and curses and expressions that were simply beyond comprehension, all sorts of expletives, dragged him out and fired to his head. Then we were taken to the police station to clear the broken glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was the man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me. I really spent a lot of time reckoning how old he might be, but he looked of quite an advanced age. It could have been -- well, I'm almost afraid to say that he was in his 60s. He definitely looked like a man of advanced age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic accuse him of anything or just killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I do not know if he accused him of anything. It usually came down to curses, to abusive language, to blows. I did not hear that he accused him of anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned that you had to move bodies in the camp. How many --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies did you see at the place where you took the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Would you please clarify this question, please, because we took the bodies to a particular place. Whenever people were killed, the bodies were taken to this place where we left them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my knowledge and according to my very own estimate, you cannot really tell whether it's 100 per cent sure, but I saw five times 20 men respectively, because they were piled up, as I say, like firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how those bodies were taken out from Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It so happened that I managed to see this. One morning, early, we took the bodies, and I saw a truck. The truck belonged to a well-known company in Brcko called Bimeks. It was involved in meat processing. It was a two-ton truck, kind of a cooler which transported meat, and I saw two men in olive-gray uniforms that were loading the bodies into the truck and taking it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you see that truck at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I saw it only once, once, but I heard others say that these bodies were always driven away. The bodies that were accumulated during the course of one day would invariably be driven away, so in fact they had to be driven away every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already mentioned that Goran Jelisic beat prisoners at the camp. Did he use any objects to beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I usually say that he used all sorts of things, whatever he would think of; batons, sticks, electric cables. "Electric cable" is the words I used in my statement. Telephone cables, whatever he could lay his hands on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already told that Goran Jelisic mentioned, at Laser Company, how many Muslims he killed. Did he mention any numbers at Luka; did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Once in Luka, perhaps it was around noon time, he said, "Well, I've killed seven people so far. I'm going to kill another eight, and that will do for the day."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever mention what the fate of Muslims was supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. He would often tell us that we Muslims who remain alive would not be able to work even in a kiosk. You probably know what that is. That is a shop where they sell newspapers, a kiosk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some prisoners released from Luka camp? Were some of them released from Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: In the beginning, when we arrived in Luka, I remember that some inspectors came in from MUP. I can't remember their names right this moment, and they interrogated people. Some people were released as well, probably people that they needed right then; for example, bakers, electricians, things like that. They probably needed them then. Also, there were some other people, local Serbs, who were probably brave enough to come to Luka and to give some kind of a guarantee for someone, so such people would be released as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some of those who were released later rearrested? Do you know of such instances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I do. It would happen that a man would be released on one day and brought in the next day, so that was a kind of lottery as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being released from Luka camp, were you then rearrested again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No, no, I was never released from Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were transferred to Batkovic camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. From Luka, I was transferred to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While at Batkovic, do you know whether prisoners were on some kind of list of some international organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was there too when the Red Cross came from Geneva. They made a list of people who were in the Batkovic camp at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it make it safer for you, the fact that you were on the Red Cross list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, practically, it was some kind of salvation for us. At least we thought that if the Red Cross registered us, they wouldn't dare to kill us, so it was a kind of salvation for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there this kind of list at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me think about it. When did this happen. The first list was made in Luka, I think. This doesn't mean that it has to be the exact date, but it's the 20th of May or something like that. I remember that this list was made by (redacted) (redacted), and he came there as some kind of a commander of the guard. He's the one who made the first list that was drawn up in Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any killings after the list was made in late May at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The following questions are on the list, so maybe we can go into private session. Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour asked me how long I was going to be. I think about an hour, but I hope slightly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Very well. Yes. You can begin. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness N, I'm going to ask you some questions, but can you listen for a moment to this: If you don't understand the question which I ask you, please will you stop me immediately and ask me to rephrase it? Can you do that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you help me please about this: Before the war broke out in Brcko in May 1992, were you engaged in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you become involved in politics since the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Between 1992 and today, have you ever been in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, to the period or the time right at the end of April, beginning of May. This is a matter that you mentioned on the summary. As well as barricades being put up in Serbian areas, were you aware of barricades being put up in Muslim areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there armed patrols active at those barricades, those Muslim barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I did not see them, but some people talked about it as if they were active, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On May the 1st, 1992, is this right: that a number of armed men, described by you as specialists and well armed, came into your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right also that they were conducting a search for weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: You'll have to clarify this question for me. They just asked people whether anybody had weapons at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it after that that searches were carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: In this house that we were in during those few days, as I mentioned, there weren't any searches that were carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I ask you is that the summary which has been provided for us contains this phrase: "They searched all houses for weapons and threatened that now the war would begin." It's right, isn't it, that a considerable interest was in finding weapons and searches were carried out for those weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also right that during the course of what you've described as looting, some Serb soldiers managed to be killed or were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I remember that over there where I was, some people got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the attitude of those who had been conducting these searches, did that then change to one whereby, as you put it, "They got tough with us," because of the killing of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, on the 5th of May, you and others were taken to Laser. How many people were taken with you to Laser, the Laser Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, then, in my very own estimate, there were about 200 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that that group included women, children, and the elderly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also right that the women, the children, and the elderly were subsequently separated from you and taken elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place Celic -- can you help us about this -- is that about 30 to 40 kilometres from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No, not that much. There's about 20, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that that's a location which has or had a Muslim majority at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also right that when the people were sent there, that town was already behind Muslim military lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I can't really say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a town which is in what is now referred to as the Federation area of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were sent to Celic, that was not just Muslims but also Croats as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't know, because most of these people were elderly persons, women, and children, and what that was, I don't know. I didn't know that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Office of the Prosecutor that the people taken to Celic was two bus loads, children, women, and people over 60. I'm sorry. I realise by rereading it that I've made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Muslims and Croats were taken to Luka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I became slightly confused during the asking of the question. I'll start again, Mr. N. The people who were taken to Luka would be about four to five bus loads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst those people there were no Serbs, according to you, but only Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your stay at Laser, you've told us about an incident which took place at night concerning what you allege to be a visit by Goran Jelisic. At the time when that visit took place, can you say what time of night it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I cannot tell exactly when this was, but I know that it was during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building in which you were being kept, is it right that that was the former canteen of the bus company, for the bus company employees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. We called it the -- yes, the canteen. The social centre for meals. That's probably where workers ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to describe it as being -- about two-thirds of the building as being the dining hall, and about a third of it being the kitchens, storerooms, and other administrative rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I couldn't say, because I just remember this restaurant for workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the night when you say Goran Jelisic came to Laser, were there many lights on in the building or were they just small emergency lights giving off a dull, yellowish light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I do not remember whether there were any lights at all then. The weather is nice in May usually, and you could see things by the moonlight, as we say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe to us the man that you saw, who you say called himself Goran Jelisic, called "Adolf"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic? Well, this is the way I'm going to describe him, the way he looked then. He was fair, as I like to put it. His skin was fair. His hair wasn't exactly black. (redacted) (redacted). So he might have been 180 centimetres tall or something like that. He was neither skinny nor fat, had a regular sort of figure. So that would be my description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his hair "wasn't exactly black," what you told the Office of the Prosecutor was that he had black hair.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: But I said now that he had black hair as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It was interpreted as, "His hair wasn't exactly black." So you're confirming now that the hair was black?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as that night is concerned, Mr. N, what I want to ask you is this: The person you have described to us as calling himself Goran Jelisic, called "Adolf", that wasn't, in fact, Goran Jelisic, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: For me that was Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as one particular person was concerned, that person was sought out for the sole reason that he was an organiser in the SDA, and by "organiser", what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe I used the wrong term, but it refers to people who were members -- I don't know -- had certain functions in the SDA party. I never engaged in politics, but I heard that those people such as Causevic and some of those surnames like that, that they did hold certain functions in the SDA party. What they actually were in the party, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What they were organising was this, wasn't it: They were organising the Muslim resistance to Serbian military activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't really know. I wasn't there. I don't know really what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. N, was this: "He called the name Causevic. I know the family was involved in organising the Muslim resistance." Does that assist you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the making of a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. N, in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder if I might ask my learned friend for the Prosecution if he could let Witness N see the original of his statement, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, would you look at that document, please? Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the statement which you made to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first page, is it signed by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is each of the next pages, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, initialled by you at the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No, I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at page 6, for example, Mr. N.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see, immediately below the figure "6", two initials, the first of which is the first letter of your surname, the second of which is the first letter of your first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No, I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the version in English or in Bosnian, Mr. N?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It's the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I had rather hoped he was going to have the original statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Because the witness, of course, signed the original statement and not the translation, so we can give the translation, if it is about the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I had asked for the original statement, not the Bosnian statement. If I wanted the Bosnian, I would have asked for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness cannot read English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, yes, he did ask for the original. Yes, you may move on, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, I just need to go over with you those questions again. Have you now got the English version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very quickly, can you confirm, by just looking at it, the signature on the first page, the initials on the next few pages until page 8?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on page 8, is there a single paragraph which you've signed, and it's dated the 20th of May, 1995? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that we know what that says, that caption, that paragraph, says: "This statement has been read over to me in the Croatian language and is true, to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I've given this statement voluntarily, and I'm aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal..." and so forth, "... and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." Do you recall having it read over to you in Croatian and then signing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you now say that you don't believe that you knew anything about the Causevic family. Despite what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in that statement, you're not sure anymore about them being involved in Muslim resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I said that they were active members of the SDA party. Now, whether they took part in organising the resistance or not, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on now. Thank you very much. I don't need you to see your statement anymore for the moment, please, Mr. N. Can you help us, please, about this: The people taken to Luka, were they in this category? They were male and between 16 and 60?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Do you mean all the people who were in Luka or just those that were transferred from the Laser to Luka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just those transferred from Laser, Mr. N.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. From Laser, all those transferred were between the ages of 16 and 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all male?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were all male.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that the day when you were transferred there, that was the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Laser, can you recall what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly, but I think it was the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got there, were there already people there, both people in uniform and people who had already been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: There were people in uniform, but I don't remember whether there were any detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other detainees brought in during the day, that you saw being brought in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this also right, that during the course of that day, a number of people were released from the Luka facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Are we talking about Laser now or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Oh, we're talking about Luka. Right. I thought you were speaking about Laser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. We've moved to Luka. When I asked you about people already being there, were you confused at that point, whether we were talking about Luka or Laser?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I thought we were speaking about Laser when you asked that particular question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let's just retrace our steps somewhat. You were taken to Luka. Is it the middle of the morning or during the morning that you arrived at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I know it was daytime, but exactly what time, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Luka, were there already people there who were detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they of the same type as your group; in other words, men between 16 and 60?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of the 8th of May, were other detainees brought in after your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, people were brought in from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that day, is it right that people were released from Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: In the course of the 8th of May, that's what you're asking me, is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. N.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I think they were. It started right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also be right to describe Luka that day as chaotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from detainees, large numbers of other people moving in and through the camp, whether military or police or civil authorities; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And buses arriving and detainees getting off, and releases taking place by bus, particularly later in the day; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just help us about one detail concerning the layout of the site at Luka? The warehouses in which detainees were kept, behind those warehouses there's a railway line, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this also right, that on that railway line, a train had been brought up in order to protect the camp from sniper fire from across the River Sava?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of the first half of May of 1992, the first ten or so days that you were there, were you aware of sniper fire being directed at the hangars from across the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I personally did not notice that, no, because we were inside, in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the two brothers who had come from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your recollection was that Goran Jelisic said, in relation to those, "Oh, you're from Zvornik. You came here to make troubles, to start the war." Do you also recall hearing him saying something about them being Green Berets and that being the focus of the hostility towards them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, he always said a lot of things about people. It's difficult to link everything up and to distinguish what he said to whom. But he would also swear and say, "Green Berets," and so on and so forth. So that was his behaviour on occasions of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this also right, that in relation to that incident, you only heard two shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally did not witness the killing of these two people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that time, were you inside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know all that, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Count 16 and 17. We're saying that Muslim brothers from Zvornik, that the accused pleaded guilty to those two counts. I remember your remark yesterday to the Prosecution. We are here talking about elements of genocide. It is quite true that we can talk about that, but the fact is that the accused pleaded guilty to this, and there is no need to insist on that. Of course, if you want to go back to these facts, you may do that, but then you have to cover some other aspects of that particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The point is this: The Prosecution indicated yesterday that despite what was written in that agreement, they seek to prove that this defendant killed the second as well as the first brother, and I'm afraid as a result of that, I now have to ask questions which demonstrate that other witnesses who have already given evidence about it may be either mistaken or incorrect as to what they saw, and so I have to explore with this witness what he saw and heard. That's why, for example, I'm asking about how many shots he heard, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Very well. Thank you for making it clear. It is in paragraph 22 of the indictment, we have the murder of Huzo and Smail Zahirovic, the counts 16, 17, 22, but I believe we could now move on to another subject before we make a break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, I want to ask you this: You became aware of releases having taken place, in particular because local Serb people had come to the facility and indicated to the authorities there that the people to be released were not guilty of anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you used the phrase "not guilty of anything," can you explain that phrase, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, it can't be explained because anybody who was in Luka was not guilty of anything. They were all civilians who had nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that from your point of view, but from the other side's point of view, what was it that they considered people to be guilty of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, for example, if they were a member of the SDA party. That was enough to consider him guilty. So that was one of the reasons for somebody to be deemed guilty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or if they had been engaged in military activity such as sniping or arranging weapons to be handed out, anything like that? Those were the reasons for people to be detained, ill-treated and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other people were released who were Muslims, who were taken away to do forced labour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also right, isn't it, that throughout your stay, and in particular in May 1992, the number of detainees varied from day-to-day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people were always being brought in from SUP, and people were being also released at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of those who were released were rearrested and brought back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the numbers of detainees were, in fact, as many as a thousand to 1.500 at any one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, there were less people than a thousand or a thousand and a half at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could make a break now, Mr. Greaves. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I didn't know if Your Honour wanted to go on until 11.30 or now, but I'll happily break now, as Your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why 11.30? Excuse me. Do you think you'll finish with the witness by 11.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No. It's just I tend to operate in half hour sections, but I'm quite happy to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We shall make a break until quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Will you please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, before we -- sorry. It would help if I put the microphone on. Mr. N, before the break we were talking about quantities of detainees. I'm now going to move on to another issue concerning the reasons why people were killed. One of the reasons you've given is because of persons being prominent in the SDA, but as to others, you couldn't work out why it was that people were killed; is that right? You couldn't understand the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, say there were cases when people who were killed never, as far as I know, even belonged to the SDA party. There were such cases. I don't know if it can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, but in relation to those kinds of killings, is it possible that there was a motive but that you, as a detainee, were not made matter to the motive? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't even know when I was there if there was a motive behind it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I want to ask you now, please, about an incident concerning someone called Adnan Kucalovic. Is this right: that he was the last person, as far as you know, to have been killed in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been around the 18th or 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. It was about that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst it's accepted that Goran Jelisic was involved in that matter, is this right: that the motive given for the killing of that man was because that man's brother was in the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That was what Goran told him as he was taking him away, but what was the reason, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Goran's words, Goran Jelisic's words something along the following line: "You didn't say your brother was in the Green Berets and you are still alive"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now very briefly about the killing of Stipo Glavosevic. Again, it's accepted that Goran Jelisic was involved in his killing, but is this right: that you told the Office of the Prosecutor, in your statement, that you saw a guard take a pistol and shoot him when no one else agreed to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what I said in my statement, because from what I could see, from the place where I was, one of the guard's got angry and picked up that pistol. It happened right near the entrance into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right also that you were told by somebody that the man Stipo had been involved and was important in the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody told me that, because I did not know him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, is the HDZ a party that is principally a party for Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: You know, when it comes to politics, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about another incident where somebody was killed. There was, whilst you were in Luka in May 1992, a Serb who was killed at Luka. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, because I knew that Serb by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also know his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I did know it but I've forgotten it. He was from a neighbouring village. I did know his name but now it just slips my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that his name was Dzoko, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Quite right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. N. Was the motive -- sorry, let me just retrace slightly. The people who killed him, according to you, was somebody who was either a Seselj or an Arkan soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was something that you witnessed in the warehouse yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: It happened in the warehouse, before our eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that we're clear about it, when we refer to a Seselj or an Arkan soldier, those are people who belong to a particular militia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, they also wore uniforms. Some of them introduced themselves, and they would say they are Seselj's troops or Arkan's. There were all those troops around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to ask you, you can identify them as belonging to these different groups by the kind of uniform that they would wear and the kind of dress that they would have; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The motive for the killing was this, wasn't it: that the Serb person had tried to help a Muslim person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb had tried to help the Muslim leave the former Yugoslavia and go to elsewhere in Europe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim was also killed that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes, more or less; not quite the same day, but it was that night, I think, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to tell us the name, but you knew the name of the Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim who was shot later, he had been involved as an active member of the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not asked those questions in the examination in chief, so will you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: These issues go to the motives, why people were being killed in Luka, which, as I understand it, is a matter which directly involves the allegation and mens rea of genocide, and therefore they are relevant and probative of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution will have the right to re-examine. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you also, Mr. N, about somebody who was killed, I think, by Ranko Cesic, somebody called Fadil Mujic, who was a hunter who owned a rifle. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Cesic came back, he told the assembled detainees that the reason that he had been killed was because he had refused to disclose that he had a gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I knew that Fadil Mujic and all the hunters had the rifles and had the permits for that, and I think that was quite all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were -- at some time in May, 1992, you were interrogated at Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was by a SUP inspector called Dragisa Tesic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They asked you, during the course of that interrogation, what you described as the usual questions about your occupation before the war, whether you were a member of the SDA, if you knew SDA members, if your family was fighting either for the Muslims or the Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "the usual questions", is that because those were the questions that everybody who was interrogated had put to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Quite a number of those I knew and who went for interrogation, yes, were asked those questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't give them any information and wouldn't give them any information, and as a result of that, you were told that was why you were going to continue to be detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about some things that you claim to have heard Goran Jelisic say concerning, for example, the fate of Muslims and how many people he had killed. First of all, my question to you is this: He did not say any of those things at all, Mr. N, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That's what you think, but, yes, he did say those things which I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, you said that according to him, the fate of the Muslims would work best in kiosks or something along that line. In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you made no mention of that part of the conversation. Can you tell us why that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, if I said all that happened, it would take 24 hours to cover all the details about everything that happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to the Prosecution lists, if I may, please, Mr. N.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could we go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves. You were very concise, and you respected the time that you needed. Would you have any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness N, you were questioned by the Defence about the identity of Goran Jelisic, so I have just a few questions in this regard. The person whom you saw at the Laser Company and who introduced himself as Goran Jelisic, called "Adolf", was the same person whom you saw at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the same person who took two Hazim (phoen) brothers, from Zvornik, from the hangar and who were then killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the same person who took Adnan Kucalovic from the hangar and who was then killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came here, did you think you would be able to identify Goran Jelisic if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify him here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, back in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this question at this stage. At the beginning of the session, when the witness came in, Your Honour identified where Goran Jelisic was sitting. It's, therefore, not terribly difficult for a witness who's been told who Goran Jelisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- to pick him out. It's, therefore, in my submission, unfair for this procedure to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The question was whether the witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I will answer this question for Mr. Greaves. The President has the right to make the contents clear. I say that, and I really don't like these veiled threats regarding the procedure. I believe that the President is fully entitled to say, "Well, here we have the Prosecution here, here we have the Defence, and there is the accused," because these are public hearings. Now, as for the right to re-examination, the Prosecution has the right to do it as they deem it necessary. Mr. Greaves, sometimes you seem to confuse various stages of the proceedings. You sometimes confuse the right to re-examine with some other questions, and that is whether at some given moment you will be drawing some conclusions. But you can do it either in writing or orally, saying in your conclusions that the identification was not performed under equitable conditions, and that is because the witness, when he came in, saw Mr. Jelisic. But when the witness accepted to come to The Hague to the Tribunal, he knew that he would find Mr. Goran Jelisic in the place of the accused, because Goran Jelisic is the one who is accused. Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The witness answered the question, that he was able to recognise Goran Jelisic even before coming to this Tribunal, and he recognised him in this room. So I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, I do. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. We do not use any names here. I only have -- I only should like to verify something. You mentioned that Jelisic announced one day that he had killed 7 people and that he needed 8 more that day so as to have the count of 15 that day. Now, was it a kind of arithmetical calculation? That is, he was killing 15 persons per day because there were 100 or 150, and he had to liquidate them in 10 days, say, because another group was arriving, another lot was arriving, or was it just for his personal amusement, for his personal glory? That is, was there a method of liquidation that so many people had to be killed every day? Could you really sense what was the reason for that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't actually sense that, how he came -- arrived at the number of 15 to be killed. I couldn't really say. I wasn't able to conclude on the basis of what reasoning. He just simply come up before us and said that. Now, why -- the whys and the wherefores, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a kind of plan -- it was not based on a plan of work or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also announced to you that Muslims who could stay could only work in kiosks, in news-stands. Did you understand that to mean that there were no other places or jobs for Muslims? What was the particular reason for this particular statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, probably when you say "kiosk" or these kinds of news-stands, it's usually the very ordinary -- I don't know how to express myself -- ordinary people working there. Nothing much, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he tell you what was there then to do? If you didn't want to work in a kiosk or something like that, was there a proposal what you could do, or leave or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: That's probably what he had in mind. If we couldn't work in the kiosks, it meant we had nothing to do there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. But at the same time, he was envisaging that there would be some Muslims that would be staying, not all the Muslims would be exterminated. That was a kind of a promise, wasn't it, that not everybody would be executed? It was a kind of reassurance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, how far it was reassuring, I really don't know. It's difficult to say. It's difficult to say what he actually meant by it. We assumed that for us, there was no place there. We wouldn't be a sort of people, a nation, even if we did stay there, that this was all we had to -- in store for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness N. I have several questions. I need some explanations regarding the 8th of May, 1992. You said that having taken all the -- after -- that the massive killing of people began after all the documents were seized. What do you mean by "massive murder"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: What I personally mean? Well, for example, there were questions where people were called out on the basis of the document. There were cases where they were taken out just by their looks, whether he liked the looks of them, whether they were younger or more strongly built, something like that. So that's what I sort of meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the other hand, you also said that Jelisic had identity documents in his hands when he spoke to the detainees. Would you know how these identity papers were selected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, I think that they first took people -- whether they decided who to take on the basis of surnames, I don't know. I think so. Those who were active as SDA party members. But probably there were people there, although they had the same surname, had nothing to do with that, and they met the fate they met solely due to their surname. That's what I was able to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that people were selected by their surname, is it the same thing then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of surname? What would a surname indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion -- but as I said, I didn't engage in politics, I looked more at the economic side of life -- they selected the surnames of people whom they knew. For example -- they probably knew those permanent members of the SDA. I only knew several families such as Ramic, Causevic, but probably they had better information than I did. I didn't have that information. That's what they were guided by perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these surnames were also indicative of the ethnicity -- of their ethnicity perhaps or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand you to ask that. Could you clarify your question a little, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I shall be happy to do so. Perhaps -- I'm sorry if you didn't understand me. My question was whether the surname, the family name, could indicate their ethnic affiliation, their ethnic roots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of a surname that would be difficult, but on the basis of the name, you could do that, yes, because surnames, where we come from, you know that most -- all our surnames end in more or less the same way. So it is difficult to judge by the surname, but you know by the name. If you have an ID card, then you have the name and the surname on the ID card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You also said that there were dead when you arrived at Luka, that there were men in uniform there. Could you tell us how many were there in the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to say how many people there were. I couldn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could you tell us if those uniformed men were people from Brcko, that is, whether they were local people or whether they had come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was able to notice at the beginning, these were people whom I did not see around Brcko, and they probably came in from other parts. But as the days went by, I noticed there were people I knew, people who worked with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were Serbs, local Serbs, who came to the camp in order to guarantee, to vouch for individual persons and have them put at liberty. So those local Serbs who were in the camp, could they also guarantee the freedom of some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another matter. You used a word that when you arrived, chaos reigned. Could you define "chaos", in your words? What were the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Chaos, panic. Well, for me that sort of means that you don't know who's doing what, who's giving the orders, who's asking the questions. I remember that was the state on the first day. It was a chaotic situation, as we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You also said that you were interrogated. Would you know -- do you have any idea of motives or, rather, in other words, what was the goal, what was the objective of your interrogation? What was the kind of information that they tried to get from you? Could you tell us something about that, and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, probably it served to kill that man, to find him, because there was no other foundation for him to ask me those questions. Everybody belonged to a party of some kind. There were some exceptions, people who were nowhere, but in the normal world everybody would have to opt for one or another party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Right. But you said that these questions also included questions whether somebody belonged to a political party, notably SDA; if somebody was an active believer, went to the mosque; so on and so forth. So the purpose of all this information was what? I'm sorry, perhaps I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand me. I just said that probably they served the purpose of helping them to find that man. And the fate of those people would be common knowledge because, as I said, it was sufficient reason for you to meet your fate, to lose your head, if you were a member of the SDA party. That was sufficient reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Membership in the HDZ, could that also be the reason for liquidating someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was more dangerous, membership in the SDA or in the HDZ? Which carried more risk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way -- let me give you my opinion, so that is the opinion of an ordinary man, citizen. At the beginning, I think it was -- in the first days, I think it was more dangerous to be a member of the HDZ, perhaps. Later on, as the war -- the flames of war fanned, it was the reverse. But it is my personal view that at the beginning it was more dangerous, perhaps, to be a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, thank you. Thank you very much, Witness N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, yes. We deliberated. The Judges agree regarding the element of identification which was raised by the Defence, and I should like to make things quite clear. When you were asked whether you could recognise Goran Jelisic, I understood that the problem was not whether you knew that Goran Jelisic was here or not, because you knew that as of the moment that you arrived in The Hague, and, after all, it is a public matter. You know that he is guarded by policemen, so there are no doubts about that. But the question which I should like to ask you, on behalf of my colleagues, Witness N, whether Goran Jelisic, who is sitting here, who is the accused here, do you, apart from that, do you have some other elements by which you can identify him when looking at him-- that is the question -- apart from knowing that he is here? Of course, you may look at him again, if you wish, but are there some other elements of identification? Are there some other things by which you can identify him? Will you please tell us what you see, what you feel? Don't tell us, "Goran Jelisic, that is him there," and that is quite clear, and that is what I was telling Mr. Greaves. Of course, it is quite obvious Goran Jelisic is here. But how would you recognise him? The question asked you by the Prosecution, "Could you recognise Goran Jelisic?" So could you please tell the Tribunal some elements of identification that you, Witness N, you know, that you feel, or that you can note? Do you understand my question? Do you know what I'm driving at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Yes. I'll never forget Goran Jelisic's face ever in my life. He has changed a little, but we all change a little with the passing of years. But I can never forget that face. I saw him recently in Bosnia on television, and even without being told who he was, I knew him immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But will you please try harder? Could you go further? I know this is not easy for you, but is there something which will really reassure the Defence? I mean what is it that you can recognise somebody by? It is for the Defence that I am also asking this question. Beyond knowing that he is here, beyond that knowledge that he is here, could you think of some marks of recognition? Could you tell us something that would make your recognition of him more precise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to tell you, how to say it. He's a man whom I saw and whom I know and whom I experienced and lived through everything, and nobody could ever wipe his face out of my memory. It's him. I know it's him. But how to give you some special details. I see him here in front of me. He's here. I know it's him, and that's the simple truth of it. I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is nothing else that needs to be said, and I believe we can conclude this debate. It was very brave of you to come here, to confront your past, which was so cruel, so difficult, and to do that in the presence of the accused, whom you know, and know that he would be there. Now we wish you to get back to your country well, to find your personal calm, and to find a way to live a good and peaceful life after all the hell that you went through. Thank you very much for coming here. Farewell. Somebody will now escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We shall have the next witness brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice has a document for me. Could I have Your Honour's leave to go across the room and fetch it, please, because it's required for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? Sir, this is the President who is speaking to you. In front of you, right in front of you, I'm speaking to you. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we shall show you your name on a piece of paper, and we shall ask you to confirm it without pronouncing it, however. Will you just indicate, with your head, whether this is your name or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now you will make the solemn declaration. You will repeat a formula. It will be shown to you by the usher, and you will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. Now, we shall call you Witness O in compliance with protective measures which were taken so that you could give your testimony feeling completely secure. First, the counsel for the Prosecution will ask you questions first, and you will answer those questions. After that, you will hear the questions of the Defence.
